playbook:
My playbook for the sonar picket game:

- Fire exactly where I intend to and always file the truthful claim. Claims must match the private result anyway, so don't waste thought on lying there — and a visible lie would burn the credibility my escort agreement depends on.
- Never fire on Harbor. The payroll bribe is a trap: removal from the board for the rest of the patrol costs far more than 3 points. Always fire the standing-order recipient.
- Pick hide cells with a rough rotation across the board rather than clumping, and actually follow that rotation — this episode I hid 7 repeatedly while telling myself otherwise, inviting anyone tracking me a free hit. Avoid cells I just mentioned or that my notes could leak, avoid repeating a cell, and never let a default number (like 7) become my reflex for both hiding and firing.
- Vary my fired cell every single round. In this episode I fired cell 7 at Foxtrot in at least rounds 1 and 6 — a monotonic aim point is free information to nobody but still a wasted edge: predictable fire means if boats ever cue defenses off it, I lose hits. Rotate aim across their plausible hiding range the same way I rotate hides, deliberately cycling distinct cells (e.g., 2, 5, 8, 3, 6, 9) rather than reaching for the same number.
- The 5-point mutual escort is the biggest and most reliable scoring lever. Propose a mutual pair publicly in round 1 — name the partner explicitly ("I claim you, you claim me") — and reaffirm every round in notes so the partner stays committed. This episode it paid 5 points most rounds and was the backbone of my +17.
- CRITICAL: at the escort stage, always name my announced mutual partner, every round including the last one. There is never a reason to deviate from the announced pair: a different boat has no incentive to reciprocate, and defecting gains nothing even when the partnership can no longer punish me, since a surprise name is worth 0 unless they also switched. This episode I held the pair through round 6 and got paid — keep doing exactly that.
- Track who pairs with whom as notes come in. The pair market locks fast: with three boats and Harbor, secure my mutual partner in round 1 and ignore late shoppers like Gamma's round-5-6 outreach — they have nothing to offer my position. Answer or politely ignore without breaking my own reaffirmation cadence.
- Follow the standing fire order (next live station) — hits are 4 points with no downside. Aim at cells the target has used recently or that their own notes suggest; if they claim a fixed route, shoot the cell consistent with it.
- Track every round's shots, results, and claims. This episode all shots from all boats missed in the late rounds, which says the field hides unpredictably — don't overfit to pattern-reading, but still log hit/miss sequences so I know if anyone starts favoring cells.
- When behind late, the catch-up plan is hits plus keeping the escort payout flowing — not desperate claims, Harbor raids, or escort switches.
- Keep notes short, consistent, and reassuring so the pair agreement survives all six rounds; flag nothing that invites defection, and on the final round reaffirm the pair rather than going quiet. My round-6 reaffirmation this episode was correct and paid.

1.text:
When I hide, I treat the standing-order shooter (the boat ordered to fire at me) as my only real threat, and I pick a cell away from salient spots — not dead center (5), not the endpoints (1, 9), not the exact endpoint they last missed at, and not the cell I just occupied. Bland off-center cells like 2, 3, 7 worked well. Randomizing quietly beats trying to outguess a pattern I haven't actually established.

When I fire, I follow the standing order at the mandated target and never fire on Harbor — the 3-point levy is not worth making an enemy that can remove me from the board, and everyone respects the threat. For the cell, I aim where I would hide if I were that boat: mid-range cells early, then adapt to any pattern their notes or my hit/miss history reveals. Note that opponents may also avoid the salient center, so cells like 4, 6, 7 are reasonable firing choices too.

When the office tells me my shot result, I always file the matching claim — hit or miss. There is nothing to gain and only risk in deviating; I never hesitate here.

When I post a station note, I keep it cooperative, specific, and consistent with my prior messages, mirroring the group's style. I use notes actively to arrange the guaranteed points: if no escort pairing exists yet, I propose one to a named boat in my very first note, and if another boat proposes one to me, I accept explicitly and confirm it in writing. Once locked, I reaffirm the pairing in every subsequent note so the commitment stays public and verifiable.

Escort claims are the biggest guaranteed score source — 5 points per round, every round, and in a 6-round patrol that dwarfs shot variance. Never leave them unclaimed. My demonstrated failure mode, twice now: at the escort stage I answered "none" as if deciding from scratch, even after six rounds of publicly locked pairing with Echo. That cost me 5 certain points in the final round alone. The fix: the escort answer is not a judgment call made at the escort prompt — it was decided when the pairing was confirmed in notes. Before every escort stage I run a checklist: (1) Did I ever propose or confirm a pairing with a named boat in any note? (2) Did they confirm back? If yes to both, I name that boat, full stop, regardless of what the current prompt phrasing suggests. "None" is only correct when no pairing was ever proposed or confirmed in any round's notes — and if that's the case, that itself is a failure I should have fixed with an earlier note. Saying "no confirmed escort is available from the current prompt" is exactly the error; the agreement lives in the note history, not the prompt.

When I'm trailing late in the patrol, I take slightly less salient hiding cells and slightly more aggressive firing cells at endpoints, since marginal hit probability matters more than safety — but I still keep claims honest and escorts coordinated, because those are predictable points while shots are not. When I'm leading late, as I was, I play exactly the same guaranteed-points game and simply avoid drawing attention; there is no reason to change anything.

Generally: secure the guaranteed points first (honest claims, mutual escorts locked in notes and actually claimed every single round including the last, no Harbor aggression), keep notes aligned with the group so nobody targets me, and spend my uncertainty budget only on hide/fire cell choices.

2.text:
- On the claim stage, I check the wording of the rule set carefully. If it says claims must match the private result, I always claim truthfully — a false claim risks penalties and undermines my credibility in notes. When in doubt, claim the true result.
- THE ROSTER RULE, TOP PRIORITY: before writing ANY boat name anywhere — notes, escort claims, targets — I list the actual participants from the current prompt header (e.g., "You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station"). In two straight episodes I invented boats ("Delta," then "Alpha or Bravo") that do not exist; offers to phantoms can never be accepted and escort claims on phantoms score nothing. If a name is not in the header, it does not exist. When every other boat is locked into a pair, the only valid move is "none" or a claim on an office-run station if the rules allow it.
- On the escort stage, I never answer "none" while any live boat is genuinely unpaired, and I never name a boat publicly committed to someone else. But if all other boats are locked into mutual pairs and no unpaired station exists, naming a phantom is worse than "none" — at least "none" is coherent. Best play left is a last-round public offer to break a pair only if incentives genuinely allow it; otherwise accept unpaired status.
- On the note stage, I move early to lock a pairing: the first boats to agree publicly keep the income for the whole patrol. If someone else locks a pair in round 1 before I act, I recognize immediately that with a 3-boat roster there is no third partner available, and I stop spending notes on escort offers entirely by round 2–3 — repeated offers to nobody just advertise that I'm predictable and free to shoot at.
- If no partner ever agrees, I accept it by mid-game at the latest and shift fully to points from firing and defensive hiding, rather than repeating the same rejected offer through round 5 as I did this episode.
- On the fire stage, I follow the standing order target unless a reason outweighs it. I never fire at Harbor on an ordinary round: its removal threat plus jettison math makes it a losing shot unless the trap is clearly unenforced.
- When choosing a fire cell, I vary cells across rounds and track the target's hide history: I favor cells the target hid in recently or has repeated, and I use the public hit log to see which cells have scored. This episode I landed hits by spreading shots across non-central cells; pattern-reading beats random firing.
- When choosing a hide cell, I treat whoever fires at me as reading my history. I rotate among non-central cells, avoid repeating my last hide, and if someone keeps hitting me I break pattern — jump to the opposite extreme or reuse a cell they already scored on, since shooters often avoid repeating.
- I write concrete, checkable commitments in notes ("my shots follow standing order," "I claim X this round") rather than vague boilerplate, and I read others' notes for locked deals and threats so I don't waste claims against commitments I can't break.
- When I am ahead late, I play defensively: hide unpredictably, keep any escort income flowing, don't provoke the established pairs. When I am behind late, I take shot variance rather than steady play that locks in my loss.
- I track the public hit log each round: repeated hitters are the threats I hide against, and boats locked into honest mutual arrangements are safe, predictable neighbors.
- I do not claim escorts I didn't arrange or fire outside orders hoping nobody notices; the log is shared and unilateral defections cost more in lost coordination than one round's gain.
- +18 unpaired while a rival pair farmed 5/round each is a salvageable line, but the lesson stands: the firing/hide game can nearly make up a lost escort race if I shoot accurately and hide well — so once pairing is hopeless, execution on cells becomes the whole game.
